newsitem.title: UK: Global oil refiner margins rise on week, U.S. lags.
newsitem.headline: Global oil refiner margins rise on week, U.S. lags.

text.p: Oil refining margins rose sharply in most of the world last week as crude oil crashed in value, but record refinery utilisation rates in the U.S. meant margins there were almost unchanged.
World benchmark Brent crude oil tumbled by $1.80 a barrel over the week to Friday to around $17.70 and while refined products fell too, their decline failed to keep pace.
Margins in the Mediterranean gained the most - with the prospect of renewed Iraqi oil sales adding downwards pressure in the region following the renewal of the U.N. oil-for-food deal.

A complex cracking refinery in the Med running Urals crude oil benefited by a rise in margins to $3.52 a barrel on Friday, a weekly rise of nearly $1.50, while a simpler hydroskimming refinery saw a gain of nearly $1.60 to $1.92, according to Reuters data calculated from standard products yields.
Margins in Singapore rose by almost as much. Complex cracking refineries and simpler hydroskimmers gained around $1.40 each to $3.47 and $1.05 respectively.

But traders expect these margins to slip again in a context of high inventories and poor demand for products. "Margins temporarily look brilliant because the products haven't caught up yet," a trader in Singapore said on Monday.
Margins in the U.S. have failed to match those in the rest of the world because of high refinery utilisation rates which have resulted in a glut of products and supportive extra demand for crude oil.
Data released by the U.S. Department of Energy showed refinery utilisation rates were 100.4 percent of nameplate capacity.

Average margins on the U.S. Gulf coast were $1.91 last week for a complex refinery running imported Brent crude oil, compared to $1.90 the previous week. For refineries running indigenous WTI crude, margins fell by five cents to 90 cents.

Margins in Rotterdam for complex cracking refineries, meanwhile, rose by around 75 cents a barrel to $2.42 for the average of last week and bearish sentiment in crude oil markets was expected to keep margins perky, with producer volumes in the North Sea expected to jump as a heavy schedule of field maintenance begins to ease from the middle of the month.
